bib.title: WARM: On the Benefits of Weight Averaged Reward Models

question: Can averaging the weights of several reward models fine-tuned from a shared pre-trained LLM give a reward model that is more reliable under distribution shift and more robust to noisy preference labels, at no extra inference cost, and so mitigate reward hacking?
hypothesis: Weight averaging of RMs approximates prediction ensembling under distribution shift while additionally reducing memorization of corrupted labels, thus delaying reward hacking.
contributions: WARM, the first instance of weight averaging for reward modeling, mitigating reward hacking, improving reliability under distribution shifts and robustness to label corruption.

Validation of linear mode connectivity for reward models on binary preference data, and a theoretical and empirical difference between weight and prediction averaging under label corruption (WA keeps only invariant predictive mechanisms across runs).
Baklava: initialise RM featurizers from different checkpoints along one SFT trajectory as a source of diversity.

method.summary: Fine-tune M PaLM-XXS reward models from a shared pre-trained/SFT model with a shared linear-probed head but different learning rates, dropout, data order and SFT-checkpoint inits (Baklava), then average their weights into one RM. Compare to single RMs and a prediction ensemble (ENS) on TL;DR summarization with AI-labelled preferences, in best-of-N and REINFORCE RL, judged by a larger PaLM-XS control RM and a PaLM-L pairwise oracle.
method.task: reward modeling for RLHF on Reddit TL;DR summarization (best-of-N and RL)

datasets.name: Reddit TL;DR (Stiennon et al.)
datasets.size: 123k posts; ~5% held out as ID validation
datasets.source: Stiennon et al. [14]; summaries generated by GPT-3 variants
datasets.preprocessing: Preference labels regenerated by PaLM-L AI labeler (RLAIF 'Detailed + CoT 0-shot', max decode 512 tokens, T=0.0, both orderings); corrupt setup swaps labels of 25% of training samples

datasets.name: D_ood
datasets.source: Summaries from multiple PaLM-XS policies at high temperature (pre-trained only, SFT-ed, RLHF-ed); labelled by same AI labeler

models.name: PaLM-XXS RM (WARM / individual / ENS)
models.architecture: PaLM featurizer + linear probed classification layer shared by all RMs
models.init_from: pre-trained then SFT on TL;DR preferred summaries for 12k steps (batch 128, Adafactor, lr 1e-5); RMs start from SFT checkpoints at steps {8k,10k,12k} (Baklava)

other.M: main clean experiments: 10 RMs trained, WARM uses the M best by OOD accuracy (M in 2, 6, 10)

models.name: Control RM (PaLM-XS)
models.architecture: PaLM-XS pointwise RM, larger and disjointly pretrained vs PaLM-XXS RMs

training.objective: Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood for RMs (Eq. 1); policy: modified REINFORCE with value-function baseline plus KL regularisation (coefficient alpha)
training.steps: RM: 10k steps; RL: curves up to about 8k-10k steps (read from Fig 1b, 18)

other.weight_selection: WARM with M weights = average of the M best RMs ranked by D_ood accuracy; Fig 10 shows best-to-worst ordering is a reliable heuristic

inference.decoding: BoN: sample N summaries from SFT policy, return highest-reward; RL samples at T=0.9
inference.samples: BoN: PaLM SFT N=8 over D=15000 prompts; T5 SFT N=1000 over D=1000 prompts. Single run per config stated; no seeds reported.
inference.prompting: AI labeler: RLAIF 'Detailed + CoT 0-shot', both orderings

metrics.name: Control reward (and gain)
metrics.definition: Pointwise score from larger PaLM-XS control RM (80.1% OOD acc); gain is relative to RM phi_1

metrics.name: Oracle preference win rate
metrics.definition: Pairwise win rate judged by PaLM-L AI labeler against reference policy/selection

baselines: Individual RMs phi_1, phi_2 (best by OOD accuracy)
ENS (prediction averaging, M=2 only for computational reasons)
eval.protocol: Clean and 25% label-corruption setups; KL to SFT policy on x-axis; no seeds, error bars or significance tests reported; no human evaluation.

availability.data: TL;DR dataset public; D_ood and AI labels not stated as released

evidence.quote: a learning rate sampled in {1e-5,4e-5,1e-4}, and a dropout probability in {0.05, 0.1}

results.claim: A policy RL fine-tuned with WARM M=6 for 3500 steps has a 79.4% oracle win rate against the policy RL fine-tuned with the best individual RM phi_1 after 3000 steps.
results.setup: TL;DR, clean labels, PaLM-XS policy, REINFORCE; WARM M=6 policy at step 3500 vs phi_1 policy at step 3000 (not matched steps); PaLM-L oracle
results.quote: the previous reference from Figure 9(b) actually has a 79.4% win rate against it.
results.note: Abstract says 'against a policy RL fine-tuned with a single RM'; the comparison is at different step counts (3500 vs 3000), each chosen as a reference, not matched-step.

results.claim: WARM M=6 RL policy reaches a 99.8% oracle win rate against the SFT policy after 3500 steps, the highest among all policies.
results.setup: TL;DR clean, PaLM-XS policy, oracle PaLM-L
results.quote: WARM 𝑀= 6 reaching a win rate of 99.8% after

results.claim: In BoN, summaries selected with WARM win up to 92.5% against random selection from SFT.
results.setup: T5 SFT generations, N up to 1000, clean and corrupt setups, oracle PaLM-L
results.quote: have a win rate of up to 92.5% against the random selection

results.claim: In RL, increasing M pushes the control-reward/KL Pareto front up and left; ENS (M=2) still hacks early and reaches lower control reward than WARM even at M=2.
results.setup: TL;DR clean and 25% corrupt, PaLM-XS policy
results.quote: increasing 𝑀pushes the Pareto front of solutions to the top left in Figures 8(a) and 8(b).

results.claim: M=10 delays reward hacking but does not improve peak performance over M=6, which the authors attribute speculatively to weaker RMs phi_7..phi_10.
results.quote: we speculate this is related to our weight selection procedure

results.claim: The optimal KL coefficient alpha for WARM is lower than for a single RM because WARM mitigates hacking so optimal policies sit at larger KL.
results.setup: RL clean, alpha in {0.001,0.003,0.01}, WARM M=6 vs phi_1
results.quote: the optimal value of 𝛼for WARM is lower than for a single RM

results.claim: Under 25% label corruption WA is far worse than ENS on corrupted training samples (less memorization) but better on OOD test data.
results.setup: Two RMs phi_1, phi_2 fine-tuned independently with same config, 25% training labels swapped, TL;DR, PaLM-XXS
results.quote: WA reduces memorization of the corrupted labels in Figure 4(a)

results.claim: In BoN, WARM beats ENS (M=2) and the two best individual RMs on control reward, with larger gains at M=6.
results.setup: PaLM SFT (N=8, D=15000) and T5 SFT (N=1000, D=1000), clean and corrupt
results.quote: moreover, the gains get bigger for 𝑀= 6

results.claim: Linear mode connectivity holds for RMs on OOD accuracy; WA and ENS accuracy curves closely match.
results.setup: Interpolating two PaLM-XXS RMs; OOD accuracies lie within about 0.758-0.765
results.quote: this is validated in Figure 3 where the accuracy curves on D𝑜𝑜𝑑for WA and ENS closely match

results.claim: The control reward model reaches 80.1% accuracy on D_ood.
results.quote: control reward reaching 80.1% accuracy on the OOD dataset

results.claim: Inter-labeler agreement for InstructGPT is cited as 72.6%.

limits: Authors concede WARM cannot combine architectures/pre-trainings as ENS can, and cannot use prediction disagreement for uncertainty.
WARM replicates shared biases such as summary-length reliance; it does not remove spurious correlations.
WARM addresses only reward modeling, not other RLHF challenges.
Single task (TL;DR), small models (PaLM-XXS RMs, PaLM-XS policy), AI-generated labels and AI oracle; no human evaluation; no seeds or error bars reported.
ENS compared only at M=2 for computational reasons; WARM compared at M up to 10.
Theory relies on simplified assumptions (orthogonal features, bag of features, binary featurizer) following Lin et al.
Reward hacking still occurs eventually under RL (control reward collapses at large KL).

terms.definition: Weight Averaged Reward Models: fine-tune M RMs from a shared pre-trained LLM, then average them in weight space.
Initialise RM featurizers from different checkpoints collected along a given SFT trajectory, relaxing the shared-initialisation constraint to sharing the same pre-training.
Pointwise reward from a larger, disjointly pretrained PaLM-XS RM used to detect hacking of the PaLM-XXS proxy.
